title: Union-find, tries and prefix matching in Java
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Union-find with int[] arrays, trie nodes with Node[26] versus HashMap children, and IPv4 longest prefix match with >>> and bit masks.
source: Oracle Java tutorials (bitwise operators); JLS 15.19 (shift operators); CLRS ch. 19-21; LeetCode Redundant Connection, Implement Trie; RFC 4632 (CIDR)

questions.prompt: Write a Java class UnionFind with int[] parent and int[] rank, a constructor UnionFind(int n), int find(int x) with path compression, and boolean union(int a, int b) that uses union by rank and returns false if a and b are already connected.
questions.explanation: The boolean return is what makes Redundant Connection and cycle detection a one-liner. Iterative path halving (parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]) is an equally good find. Recursion depth is fine with union by rank because trees stay O(log n) tall.

checks.label: has an int[] parent array initialised so each node is its own parent
find compresses the path (parent[x] = find(...) or parent[parent[x]])
union uses rank or size to pick the new root
union returns false when the roots are equal

questions.prompt: Write a Java class Trie for lowercase words with a nested Node class holding Node[] next = new Node[26] and boolean end. Implement void insert(String w) and boolean search(String w); search must return true only for complete inserted words, not mere prefixes.
questions.explanation: The end flag separates search("car") from startsWith("ca"). A HashMap<Character, Node> children map is equivalent and handles any alphabet. Insert and search are O(L).

questions.prompt: The IPv4 address 10.1.3.7 is held in a Java int as 0x0A010307. What does the expression (ip >>> 8) & 0xFF evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Shifting right by 8 drops the last octet (7); masking with 0xFF keeps the next 8 bits, which are the third octet, 3. >>> avoids sign extension for addresses of 128.0.0.0 and above.

questions.prompt: Insert car, cart, cat, dog and do into an empty trie whose nodes each hold a Node[26] array. Counting the root, how many array slots (references) are allocated in total?
questions.explanation: Shared prefixes give 8 nodes plus the root = 9 nodes; each owns a Node[26] with 26 reference slots, so 9 * 26 = 234, though only 8 of them are non-null. This is why sparse alphabets favour map-based children.

questions.prompt: You build a Java trie for autocompleting search terms in many languages (a huge, sparse alphabet). How should each node store its children?
questions.explanation: Node[26] gives O(1) indexed access for a small known alphabet such as lowercase letters; HashMap children win for Unicode.

options.text: A fixed Node[65536] array per node, because arrays always beat maps on speed and memory.
options.why: Every node would carry 65536 mostly empty slots, wasting memory.

options.text: A sorted ArrayList scanned linearly at every node.
options.why: Scanning a long list at each level slows lookups far beyond O(L).

options.text: A HashMap<Character, Node>, since most characters never occur at a node.
options.why: Correct: memory grows with the children that exist, not with the alphabet size.

options.text: A single global HashMap from full word to Node.
options.why: That loses the shared-prefix structure and the prefix queries a trie exists for.

questions.prompt: Inside a Java trie for lowercase words, which expression turns the char ch into a child index from 0 to 25?
questions.explanation: Characters are numeric in Java, so subtraction works directly. Validate the input alphabet, or you get ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

options.why: Correct: char arithmetic gives 0 for 'a' through 25 for 'z'.
The raw code of 'a' is 97, which is outside a 26-slot array.
This gives 1 to 26, so the letter z lands outside a 26-slot array.
Adding moves further above 26, so every index is out of bounds.

questions.prompt: The address 192.168.0.1 is stored in a Java int, which makes the value negative.
questions.explanation: Without the mask the two shifts differ: ip >> 31 is -1 for such an address while ip >>> 31 is 1. Use >>> when treating an int as unsigned.
questions.assertion: (ip >> 31) & 1 and (ip >>> 31) & 1 both give the top bit, 1, for this address.
questions.reason: Masking with & 1 keeps only the lowest bit, so the sign extension in the upper bits does not matter.

whys.a: Right: >> fills the upper bits with ones, but & 1 throws them away, so the two shifts agree; R is the reason.
whys.b: R is the reason, not an unrelated fact.

questions.prompt: A union-find over nodes 0..n-1 in Java.
questions.explanation: Dense integer node ids make an int[] the fastest and smallest choice; for string-keyed nodes map them to ids first.
questions.assertion: The parent links are usually stored in an int[] indexed by node.
questions.reason: Java arrays are objects allocated on the heap.

whys.a: Heap allocation does not explain why an int[] is a good fit; dense integer ids do.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but the heap detail is unrelated; the index-by-id access is what makes int[] natural.

questions.prompt: Memory use of a trie that stores 3 words.
questions.explanation: The array exists as soon as the node is created, so sparse tries waste memory; map-based children allocate per child instead.
questions.assertion: A trie node holding a Node[26] array allocates 26 reference slots even when it has a single child.
questions.reason: Java fills a new object array with empty strings until a child is assigned.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but a new Node[26] holds null references, not empty strings, so R is false.

questions.prompt: A trie stores children in a HashMap<Character, Node> and lists the words below a prefix.
questions.explanation: If suggestions must come back in sorted order, store children in a TreeMap or sort them after collecting.
questions.assertion: Iterating the children of a HashMap<Character, Node> visits them in insertion order.
questions.reason: HashMap iteration order is unspecified; LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order and TreeMap sorts by key.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is exactly why A is false; use TreeMap for alphabetical autocomplete.

questions.prompt: True or false: a recursive find on a long parent chain of 100,000 nodes can throw StackOverflowError, which is one reason to prefer union by rank or an iterative find.
questions.explanation: Union by rank keeps trees O(log n) tall, so recursion is safe there. Without it, write find iteratively (path halving) to be safe.

options.why: Correct: each recursion level uses a stack frame, and a default thread stack holds only some thousands.
Chains of that depth overflow a default stack, so the statement is true.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement with the Java type that fits best.
questions.explanation: HashMap gives O(1) exact lookup; TreeMap gives floor and ceiling in O(log n); a fixed array suits a small alphabet; int[] parent is the union-find workhorse; Java has no built-in Bloom filter, but libraries provide one.

left.text: Exact key lookup, no ordering needed
Keys in sorted order with floor and ceiling queries
Children of a trie node over lowercase letters
Connectivity of node ids 0..n-1 under merges
Approximate membership with no false negatives

right.text: Bloom filter (for example from a library)
